slides.title: Before rewarding success, make success reachable.
slides.notes:
Our goal is not just a higher math score. We want a model to learn when to use code, ask helpers, and combine their results.

Working explanation: math starts with relevant skills; our RLM asks for unfamiliar combinations. We should examine readiness to learn, not only the RL algorithm.

Next: what did the math model bring with it?

slides.title: Math RL builds on a strong head start.
slides.notes:
Pretraining supplied mathematical knowledge and examples. We added practice with checked answers, not mathematics from scratch. The same 64 questions improved from 20 to 47 correct.

This is a small-scale reproduction, not the full paper score. Prompt choice also matters: the base already solved 305 of 500 with questions alone.

Next: why is RLM use harder?

slides.title: An RLM must combine skills in a new setting.
slides.notes:
Tell the Mira example. The second helper needs Aster Lab, not an unexplained request for a city. Knowing Python does not ensure useful delegation.

Earlier training did improve some routines. The gap was reliable transfer and coordination, not zero learning. Distribution shift is a plausible explanation, not a proven cause.

Next: what practice can help?

slides.title: Useful practice is challenging, but within reach.
slides.notes:
A child without algebra needs more than a calculus test marked wrong. The analogy suggests teaching prerequisites; it does not prove models learn like children.

Walk through x = 4 versus x = 5. Our reward comparison needs contrast within one question. All right or all wrong gives zero relative signal.

Next: connect teaching to independent practice.

slides.title: Teach, practise, remove help, then test transfer.
slides.notes:
Start with a skill check, not an assumption that everything is missing. Show only what is needed, practise choices, then remove help.

In the example, first show the employer name being passed. Later ask the model to choose what information and helpers it needs.

The question is transfer, not copying a routine. This sequence still needs testing.

slides.title: Different failures need different interventions.
slides.notes:
Separate three cases. No successes: teach, simplify, improve the prompt, or try a stronger model. Rare successes: explore more varied attempts. Mixed outcomes but no gain: inspect feedback and updates.

More temperature may produce broken calls, not better plans. More retries cost compute.

Curriculum is one hypothesis among several.

slides.title: An open agenda of small experiments.
slides.notes:
These are examples, not a fixed queue or an exhaustive list. We can also explore repair, stronger models, feedback, and helper roles. Let small tests change our ideas.

Measure after preparation AND after RL. If demonstrations help but RL adds nothing, that is a teaching result.

Close: we have a direction for exploration, not a settled recipe.
